tasks.task_description: Analyze the three provided Amazon review datasets (hair_dryer.tsv, 11,470 reviews, 473 products, 2002-03 to 2015-08; microwave.tsv, 1,615 reviews, 55 products, 2004-06 to 2015-08; pacifier.tsv, 18,939 reviews, 5,432 products, 2003-04 to 2015-08) to identify quantitative and qualitative patterns, relationships, measures and parameters within and between star ratings, review text, and helpfulness ratings, that will help Sunshine Company succeed with its three new products. Scope: data cleaning, within- and between-dataset pattern extraction, and a synthesis of what should be tracked and why, all US marketplace, single time base ending 2015-08-31.
tasks.task_analysis: Data cleaning first: TSVs parsed with all 15 columns; repairs applied and counted - case-normalized vine/verified_purchase/marketplace (microwave had 7 'n'/7 'y'/'us' variants; pacifier had 7,680 'n' and 6,470 'y' plus 7,741 'us'), 1 empty headline (hair dryer) and 2 empty bodies (pacifier) kept as empty text, M/D/YYYY dates converted to timestamps (0 unparseable), numeric casts (0 bad star ratings). No duplicate review_ids; max 10 reviews per customer (pacifier). Modeling assumptions: (A1) a review's star rating and its text are the customer's contemporaneous opinion of the product, so aggregates over reviews estimate product reputation with bias only from who chooses to review (selection bias toward strong opinions - see results); (A2) products with the same product_parent form one reputation entity, and a product-level rating statistic is a sufficient summary of that reputation; (A3) the three files share one 2015-08-31 snapshot cutoff of an otherwise growing review stream (volumes grow through 2015: 3,143 hair-dryer and 5,796 pacifier reviews in 2015), so recent-window statistics are the decision-relevant ones and the sparse pre-2012 tail is baseline, not steady state; (A4) helpfulness votes are a secondary, visibility-confounded signal (they count who clicked, not how good the review is), so the primary success signal is built from star ratings and text content. The expert consultation failed in all three rounds (controller returned ok=false for exchange 1, no channel for 2-3; see interaction_evidence.md), so no externally retrieved empirical parameter enters the model; every number below is computed from the three supplied TSVs, and no external value was needed.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Variables per review r in product p at time t(r): star s(r) in {1..5}, good g(r)=1{s>=4}, low l(r)=1{s<=2}, text features x(r) (8 binary indicator classes over headline+body: enthusiastic, disappointed, quality, price, delivery, ease, safety, usage, via regex lemma lists), length w(r) in words, votes v(r)=(helpful,total). Models: (1) Category level: monthly mean rating R(m)=mean{s | month=m}, weighted OLS slope beta=argmin sum_m n_m (R(m)-a-beta t_m)^2 (t_m in months); 6-month rolling mean; drift D=mean(rolling[later half])-mean(rolling[earlier half]); per-product OLS slope for the cohort of >=8 reviews spanning >=6 months (hair dryer 122, microwave 42, pacifier 280 products). (2) Informativeness vs product-level success G(p)=share of p's reviews with s>=4: point-biserial correlation r(pb)=Pearson(log1p(measure), G) computed per candidate measure, for product pools of all products and of products with >=5 reviews (sensitivity). (3) Text-rating association: 3-level contingency (1-2, 3, 4-5) per descriptor with chi-square and Cramer's V, plus prevalence in good vs low; logistic regression logit P(g=1)=b0+sum_k b_k x_k fitted by gradient descent (L2=0.01, 4000 iters, lr=0.05, z clipped to +/-30), summarized by AUC and sign of b_k (coefficients themselves are unbounded under near-separation of enthusiastic/disappointed from the label, so AUC and sign, not magnitude, are the reported quantities). (4) Star->review intensity: median/mean body words by star level; per-product, share of the product's reviews falling after its first 1-star review within a 12-month window (146 / 42 / 93+ products, i.e. all products with a 1-star review; computed for hair dryer 146 and microwave 42). (5) Flags: share of good reviews by vine and by verified_purchase. Solution procedure: clean.py -> analyze.py (reproducible, constants on CLI: --sweep WIN=3,12 MINVOTES=1,5). Sensitivity: rolling window 3 vs 12 months left every AUC, slope and share identical (they are window-free or already at the 6-month default) and only moved the drift estimate between 0.17 and 0.35 for hair dryer/pacifier (same positive sign) and -0.02 to -0.11 for microwave (same negative sign); product pool >=5 reviews flipped the sign of the vote/text-vs-success correlations (see outcome). No empirical external parameter table is needed because the model uses no externally calibrated value.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results. (i) Measures to track, by informativeness vs product-level good-share G (point-biserial, all-product pool / >=5-review pool): the only measure strongly and consistently informative is the share of low (1-2 star) ratings: r=+0.741 (hair dryer), +0.918 (microwave), +0.772 (pacifier) with 1-G, and +0.938 / +0.979 / +0.826 in the >=5 pool - i.e. low-star share is the single best predictor of which products succeed. Vote volume and text length are NOT informative of success in the full pool (r in [-0.26, +0.05]) and, in the >=5 pool for microwave, review count flips positive (r=+0.283) while body length goes strongly negative (r=-0.53) - products that accumulate more reviews of 5-star type tend to have shorter text per review, a popularity signal, not a quality signal. Recommendation: track monthly 1-2-star share (primary alarm), rolling 6-month mean star (health), and review-velocity growth (momentum); do not track raw vote totals as a quality proxy. (ii) Time-based reputation: category monthly OLS slopes are slightly positive (hair dryer +0.0053/month, pacifier +0.0038/month) but microwave is flat-to-negative in the recent window (rolling 6-mo tail 3.73-3.78 vs head ~3.2-3.56; drift D=-0.077); hair-dryer and pacifier drift D=+0.329/+0.202 (reputation improved from the early-2000s baseline to 2015). Per-product: ~30-36% of the trended cohort has a declining slope, ~21-29% improving; worst slopes are specific failing products (e.g. Xtava Rimini hair dryer -0.282/month; Nuby nibbler -0.253/month; Samsung MC11H6033CT microwave -0.104/month) while best slopes are specific winners (Conair Travel Smart +0.048; The First Years John Deere pacifier +0.143; LG over-the-range microwave +0.086). The usable time signal is therefore product-level slope plus low-star share, not the category mean. (iii) Success/failure text+rating combinations: logistic AUC for good (4-5) vs rest: microwave 0.828 (acc 0.738), hair dryer 0.668, pacifier 0.559; for low (1-2) vs rest: 0.825 / 0.598 / 0.572. The discriminative text is emotional valence, not topic: 'disappointed/defective/terrible' language predicts low ratings (positive coefficient in the low-rating model in all three datasets, |b| largest in microwave) and 'enthusiastic/love/love/amazing' predicts good. Microwave (the appliance with the widest spread, mean star 3.45, 24.9% 1-star) is where the text+rating combination is most decision-useful; pacifier text is near-uninformative (58%+ are 5-star, AUC~0.56). (iv) Do specific star ratings incite more reviews? All reviews in all three files carry a body (share_with_body=1.0 at every star level), so the question resolves as text-length intensity: median words 51/49/43/38/29 (hair dryer) and 74/82/56/43/30 (microwave) from 1 to 5 stars - monotonically decreasing, i.e. the angrier the reviewer, the longer the review (microwave 1-star mean 109.7 words vs 5-star 62.7). Per product, reviews continue (and low stars persist) after the first 1-star review, with the post-window containing many reviews - but I deliberately do not quote a 'multiplier' from that computation because its baseline (all pre-1-star history) is confounded with product age; the defensible claim is the monotone length-by-star gradient plus the persistence of low ratings, which is what a low-star cascade alarm should watch. (v) Quality descriptors vs rating: Cramer's V - 'disappointed' V=0.415 (hair dryer, 0.485 microwave: 43-48% of 1-2-star reviews use it vs 5% of 4-5-star) and 'enthusiastic' V=0.361/0.392 (67-72% of 4-5-star vs 27-29% of 1-2-star) are the strongly associated descriptors; 'ease' is mildly positive for good ratings (V=0.108-0.219, 13-23% of good vs 4-5% of low - consistent with ease-of-use as a design-feature signal); 'quality', 'price', 'delivery', 'safety' are weak (V<=0.12) and not reliably directional. Flags: unverified purchases rate much lower (microwave good-share 0.262 unverified vs 0.759 verified; hair dryer 0.661 vs 0.785) - verified flag is a useful filter, and vine reviews skew good (0.87-0.90). Biases and limitations: review-selection bias (dissatisfied customers over-represented, which is exactly why low-star share is the strongest alarm - it is the robust part of the biased stream); helpfulness votes excluded as a quality signal (visibility confound, and 37-72% of reviews have zero votes, so the signal is spiky); the >=5-review product pool for microwaves is only 42 products, so that pool's correlations are indicative, not precise; text features are regex lemma classes, not sentiment-model outputs, so AUC bounds (0.56-0.83) rather than point predictions are reported; the common 2015-08-31 cutoff means no post-snapshot trajectory can be claimed. Most confidently recommended result: for each new product, alarm when the rolling 6-month 1-2-star share exceeds the category norm (microwave norm 25.3%, hair dryer 14.6%, pacifier 11.8%) and when 'disappointed'-class language appears in >~35% of recent low-star reviews - the microwave numbers (low-star share r=0.92-0.98 with success, text AUC 0.83, verified-vs-unverified gap 0.497) are the most statistically supported and the cleanest operational rule.
